turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.zh: Joe，你和我都是在大学——或者用你的话说，college——读的国际关系（international relations）。

turns.zh: 在 college，在 uni。是的，这对我们帮助很大。正是它让我们走到了今天这个位置。

turns.en: Yeah, I think today's guest, pretty much anyone who did any sort of political science or IR degree, or maybe even, I don't know, some undergraduate syllabus or something like that, this author, this person, was definitely on the syllabus in the early 2000s and probably still is, right?
turns.zh: 对，我觉得今天的嘉宾——基本上任何读过政治学或 IR 学位的人，或者甚至某些本科课程大纲里——这位作者，这个人，在2000年代初肯定出现在课程大纲上，现在大概也还在，对吧？

turns.en: Almost certainly still is. You know, I did all the reading back when I was in college. You know, it wasn't, even though I was... I did get a degree in it. Technically, by the way, I don't know if I've ever said this. Technically, in Texas, the degree was called government, which included poli sci and IR.
turns.zh: 几乎可以肯定还在。你知道，我在大学时把所有相关著作都读了。虽然……我确实拿了那个学位。顺便说一句，技术上——我不知道我以前有没有提过——在 Texas，那个学位叫 government，涵盖了政治学和 IR。

turns.en: You've been lying to me.
turns.zh: 你一直在骗我。

turns.zh: 这有点微妙。我没得选，它就叫这个名字。

turns.en: Insight into Joe's upcoming political ambitions.
turns.zh: 这算是对 Joe 未来政治抱负的一个洞察吧。

turns.en: That's right. But, you know, like a lot of the stuff, including the work of our guest today, I like went back and reread several years ago because I guess at the time, early 2000s, it felt a lot like theory. And then suddenly, like over the last several years, it's like, oh, this isn't just, this might help explain the world or a thing is going on in the world that I need to revisit and changes are afoot, et cetera. So I revisited the work. And so even though it was a long time ago, Feels fresh in my head.
turns.zh: 没错。但是，你知道，就像很多东西一样，包括我们今天嘉宾的著作，我在几年前重新回去读了一遍，因为当时——2000年代初——感觉更像是纯理论。然后突然之间，过去这几年，感觉就是，哦，这不仅仅是理论，这可能有助于解释世界上正在发生的事情，我需要重新审视，变化正在酝酿，等等。所以我重新读了那些作品。因此尽管是很久以前的事了，在我脑中仍然感觉很新鲜。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So I've already given it away, but today's guest is, in fact, Francis Fukuyama. He is a professor at Stanford, author of the new book, In the Realm of the Last Man, and author of famously both an essay and a book called The End of History.
turns.zh: 好吧我已经剧透了，今天的嘉宾其实是 Francis Fukuyama。他是 Stanford 的教授，新书 In the Realm of the Last Man 的作者，也是那篇著名的文章和同名书籍 The End of History 的作者。

turns.en: And The Last Man.
turns.zh: 还有 The Last Man。

turns.en: And The Last Man.
turns.zh: 还有 The Last Man。

turns.en: Which is really key.
turns.zh: 这一点真的很关键。

turns.en: Which is key.
turns.zh: 很关键。

turns.en: Which is key. So a lot of people think about The End of History as this idea that like, well, Liberal democracy has won out and we're never going to have wars or conflicts or struggles ever again. And that wasn't quite the message. And we should talk about why it kind of, I don't know, got framed in that way. But I think this whole topic clearly is very relevant at the moment because- We just had local elections in Germany earlier this month. And it's kind of a reminder that there is this lingering feeling or possibility that maybe people don't actually like the liberal order. Maybe they don't want it.
turns.zh: 很关键。很多人把 The End of History 理解为这样一种观点：自由民主已经胜出，我们再也不会经历战争、冲突或斗争了。但这并不是原著的核心信息。我们应该谈谈为什么它被那样解读了。但我认为这个话题在当前显然非常切题，因为——这个月早些时候 Germany 刚举行了地方选举。这算是一种提醒：人们心里可能仍然有一种挥之不去的感觉或可能性，即他们也许并不真正喜欢自由主义秩序，也许他们并不想要它。

turns.en: Totally. It certainly seems you can point to a lot of things. We don't need to go down the list. But various ideologies they would call like illiberalism of some form or another seem to be. on the march and there's this sort of anxiety about why and whether the people who have spent a lot of time like upholding the various institutions that we associate with Western democracy or liberal democracy entities like the EU or free trade agreements, the degree to which it feels like people are exhausted, like that there is this effort to hold it up, but there is this sense of exhaustion, maybe resignation and so forth. The one other thing I'll say before we get into it, you know, like I remember I mentioned this once or twice, but this is a thing that sticks out to me, like in middle school or maybe my first year of high school, learning about the Cold War. And it was taught in U.S. history classes. And we're talking like 93 here.
turns.zh: 完全同意。显然你能指出很多东西，我们不需要一一列举。但各种被称为某种形式的非自由主义（illiberalism）的意识形态似乎正在崛起，人们对此感到焦虑——为什么那些花了大量时间维护我们所熟知的西方民主或自由民主制度的人——比如 EU 或自由贸易协定——感觉如此疲惫。有这种努力在支撑着它，但同时有一种疲惫感，也许还有认命感等等。在进入正题之前我再说一件事，你知道，我记得我提过一两次，但这件事让我印象深刻：在初中或者高中一年级时学习冷战（Cold War）。它是在美国历史课上教的。我们说的是93年左右。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: As if it was like it might as well have been World War One. It was already taught as like.
turns.zh: 就好像它跟一战一样遥远。当时已经被当作——

turns.en: History.
turns.zh: 历史来教了。

turns.en: And now look at 20, you know, from 2026, I was like, oh, that was literally just the day before the fall of the Berlin Wall, etc. But already by that point, so many of these global questions were being taught as if they had finally been settled. Clearly nothing is settled.
turns.zh: 而现在站在2026年回头看，我就想，哦，那 literally 就是柏林墙倒塌的前一天啊。但在那个时候，这么多全球性问题已经被当作终于尘埃落定了来教。显然，什么都没有尘埃落定。

turns.en: No, that was the total vibe in the early 2000s, right? At university, it was done. And yet here we are in 2026. And it seems things are very much not finished. So without further ado... We do, in fact, have the perfect guest, Francis Fukuyama. Thank you so much for coming on Odd Thoughts.
turns.zh: 没错，那就是2000年代初的整体氛围，对吧？在大学里，一切都结束了。然而我们现在身处2026年，事情显然远未结束。所以话不多说……我们确实请到了最完美的嘉宾——Francis Fukuyama。非常感谢你来上 Odd Thoughts。

turns.en: Well, thanks very much for having me.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你们的邀请。

turns.en: When you look at something like the recent German local election, the far-right party Alternative für Deutschland, Alternative for Germany, got a majority. How do you fit something like that in your framework? Is it, well, this is a natural rejection of liberal democracy of the sort that I write about in this book, in the realm of The Last Man? Or is this just a sort of bump along the evolution of liberal democracy?
turns.zh: 当你看像最近 Germany 地方选举这样的事情——极右翼政党 Alternative für Deutschland（AfD，德国选择党）获得了多数席位。你怎么把这样的事情纳入你的框架？这是不是——就像我在书中写的那种——对自由民主的自然排斥，属于 The Last Man 的范畴？还是说这只是自由民主演进过程中的一个小坎坷？

turns.en: Well, I don't think anybody knows which of those alternatives is the right one. I think that liberal democracy has had some pretty bad moments earlier in the 20th century. The 1930s was pretty bad with communism and fascism both threatening it. The 1970s and the oil shocks also led to a lot of pessimism about the future of democracy. So it could be that we're going simply through a period like that. I think probably the discontent is a little bit more extreme this time. Freedom House says that the aggregate level of freedom in the world has declined now for the last 20 years, since about 2008 or so. And I think that one of the reasons for being more pessimistic is really what's happened in the United States, because for the entire post-World War II period, the United States was the model liberal democracy. My Chinese students 20 years ago all said they wanted China to be like the United States. They don't say that anymore. And I think that the rise of a populist movement within the leading liberal democracy in the world is a big signal that something deeper is afoot and that that discontent really reflects some underlying social changes.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为没有人知道哪种可能性是正确的。自由民主在20世纪早期经历过一些相当糟糕的时期。1930年代很糟糕，共产主义和法西斯主义同时威胁着它。1970年代的石油危机也引发了大量对民主未来的悲观情绪。所以我们可能只是正在经历类似的时期。我认为这一次的不满可能更为极端。Freedom House 说全球自由水平的总体下降已经持续了大约20年，从2008年左右开始。我认为更悲观的一个原因确实是美国发生的事情，因为在整个二战后时期，美国一直是自由民主的典范。20年前我的中国学生都说他们希望中国像美国一样。他们不再这么说了。我认为在世界领先的自由民主国家内部民粹主义运动的兴起是一个重大信号，表明有更深层的东西正在酝酿，这种不满确实反映了一些根本性的社会变化。

turns.en: I'm glad you brought up your students because actually that was sort of what I was going to ask first is, Having been a professor for several years, setting aside international students or any students, you know, like I said, when I first learned that there was this thing called the Cold War, it was just like history was settled. It had come to an end. Now, I don't think we were taught in high school that history had come to an end, but we were taught that these big questions had kind of come to an end and kind of irrelevant, kind of like in the past. And I'm curious if you've seen the evolution of your students taking your courses and what you've observed about how they view that period of time, why they're interested in it, and if their interests have changed.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你提到了你的学生，因为那其实就是我本来想先问的：作为多年教授，撇开国际学生或任何学生不谈——你知道，就像我说的，当我第一次了解到有个东西叫冷战时，感觉就像历史已经尘埃落定了，它已经走到了终点。我不认为我们在高中学到的是「历史终结了」，但我们学到的是这些大问题已经算是有了结论，变得不太相关了，属于过去的事情了。我很好奇你是否看到了选修你课程的学生的变化，你观察到他们如何看待那个时期，为什么对它感兴趣，以及他们的兴趣是否发生了变化。

turns.en: It's discouraging getting older. The Cold War is history. 9-11 is history. Even the rise of Donald Trump now is history. It happened when I was seven years old. So things move. But I think that the most important phenomenon that I hadn't anticipated is the importance of generational change. For my generation, I think the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism was the big defining event. And that's certainly what inspired me to write the end of history essay, the first one. But now we've come full circle where a lot of people that actually lived through or in those countries now want to reverse that outcome as in the Sachsen-Anhalt election. And I think that it indicates that liberal democracy actually is something that is easily taken for granted. You know, you have a couple generations since the fall of the Berlin Wall that have grown up without any knowledge of what communism really was. And I think that one of the biggest things that makes people like liberal democracy is the opposite, is living under a dictatorship. If you live in a communist dictatorship, You know, I mean, the joy that Eastern Europeans felt when communism fell was really tangible because they didn't like, you know, being surveyed and imprisoned, you know, for speaking out. And nobody experiences that in Europe or the United States or has not experienced that certainly for the last generation. And so it's very easy to assume that the good things about liberal democracy, the peace and the prosperity are just naturally there and we don't have to worry about them. And therefore, you can think about, you know, the EU as the biggest dictatorship in the world rather than a real dictatorship.
turns.zh: 变老让人沮丧。冷战已经是历史了。9-11已经是历史了。甚至 Donald Trump 的崛起现在也成了历史。它发生在我七岁的时候。所以事物在变化。但我认为我没有预料到的最重要的现象是代际更替（generational change）的重要性。对我这一代人来说，柏林墙的倒塌和共产主义的崩溃是那个定义性的大事件。这当然也是激励我写下第一篇 end of history 文章的原因。但现在我们兜了一圈回来了：很多实际经历过或在那些国家生活过的人现在想要逆转那个结果，比如 Sachsen-Anhalt 的选举。我认为这表明自由民主其实很容易被当作理所当然。你知道，柏林墙倒塌后的几代人成长过程中完全不了解共产主义到底是什么样子。我认为让人们珍惜自由民主的最大因素恰恰是它的反面——生活在独裁之下。如果你生活在共产主义独裁政权下——我是说，东欧人在共产主义垮台时感到的喜悦是非常真实的，因为他们不喜欢被监视、因为发声而被监禁。而在欧洲或美国，没有人经历过这些——至少过去一代人没有。所以很容易假设自由民主的好处——和平与繁荣——是自然而然就在那里的，我们不需要担心它们。因此，你可以把 EU 想象成世界上最大的独裁政权，而不是一个真正的独裁政权。

turns.en: Can I just ask before we get into more current events, but the end of history, I touched on it in the intro, but a lot of people interpreted that to be quite literally the end of history. So liberal democracy won, globalization won, everyone was going to trade with each other and we weren't going to have any more wars or conflict. and things like that. And I am certainly guilty in the past on this podcast of using end of history as a sort of byword for globalization. What do you attribute that misinterpretation to? Was it the zeitgeist of the end of the Cold War at the time you wrote the book in 1992? Was it people just were too lazy to read the last six chapters? What was going on?
turns.zh: 在我们进入更多时事之前，我想问一下：'历史的终结'——我在开场时提到了——很多人把它理解为字面意义上的'历史终结了'。就是说自由民主赢了，全球化赢了，所有人都要互相贸易，我们再也不会有战争或冲突了，诸如此类。我承认过去在这个播客上，我也曾经把 end of history 当作全球化的代名词来用。你觉得这种误读该归因于什么？是你1992年写书时冷战结束的时代精神（zeitgeist）？还是人们太懒了没读最后六章？到底怎么回事？

turns.en: Yeah, well, it's a little bit of all of those. The end of history was not my phrase. It was a phrase of the German philosopher Hegel, who understood history with a capital H, the way we understand today something like modernization or development. And so the idea is that human societies evolve over time, and they evolve in a progressive fashion. And so the question was, in which direction were they evolving? And that's the end, its end in the sense of goal or termination point. So the question of the end of history was, what kind of society emerges at the end of this long evolutionary process? Now for about 150 years, the Marxists took Hegel's concept of history and said the end of history is going to be communism. By the late 1980s, after Gorbachev and Puri Stryka, it seemed to me that they were never going to make it, you know, that communism was really off the table. And therefore, if there was an end of history, it was a stage just before you got to communism, which was what the communists called bourgeois democracy and a market economy and capitalism. And so for me, that was the resting point that we seem to be arriving at. What they didn't understand in the title, and I guess this is my fault for picking these words, but it was the end of history and the last man. The philosopher Nietzsche was the one that talked about the last man because he hated the idea of there being an end of history because for him, the victory of English liberalism would be a boring... flat world where nobody had aspirations. Everybody was fed, clothed, happy, but content in that happiness, just like a cow grazing in the field.
turns.zh: 嗯，以上原因都有一点。'历史的终结'不是我的说法。它是德国哲学家 Hegel 的用语，他理解的'历史'是大写的 H——就像我们今天理解的现代化（modernization）或发展（development）那样。这个理念是：人类社会随时间演化，而且是朝着进步的方向演化。那么问题是：它们朝哪个方向演化？这里的'终结'指的是目标或终点的意思。所以'历史的终结'这个问题是：在这个漫长的演化过程结束时，会诞生什么样的社会？大约150年来，马克思主义者接受了 Hegel 的历史概念，说历史的终点将是共产主义。到了1980年代末，在 Gorbachev 和 Perestroika 之后，在我看来他们永远不会成功了——共产主义真的已经出局了。因此，如果有一个历史的终点，那就是共产主义之前的那个阶段——也就是共产主义者所说的资产阶级民主、市场经济和资本主义。所以对我来说，那似乎就是我们正在到达的停靠点。人们在书名中没有理解的是——我猜这是我选词的失误——它叫 The End of History and the Last Man。哲学家 Nietzsche 才是那个谈论'末人'（the last man）的人，因为他讨厌历史有终点的想法。在他看来，英国自由主义的胜利将是一个无聊的、扁平的世界，没有人有抱负。每个人都吃饱穿暖、幸福快乐，但满足于那种幸福——就像在草地上吃草的牛一样。

turns.en: And he said- Cows seem pretty happy.
turns.zh: 而且他说——牛看起来挺开心的。

turns.en: Yeah, well, they are happy, but for Nietzsche- For a man, for a human, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，它们确实很开心，但对 Nietzsche 来说——对一个人，对一个人类来说……

turns.en: Human beings had a pride that shouldn't be satisfied just by peace and contentment, that you should want something more, you should want to dominate and so forth. And I think That's the unhappiness that I was talking about back then in that part of the book. And I think that's what's driving a lot of the extremism in the world today.
turns.zh: 人类有一种自豪感，不应该仅仅被和平与满足所安抚——你应该想要更多，你应该想要支配等等。我认为那就是我当时在书中那部分所谈论的不满足感。我认为这也是驱动当今世界许多极端主义的因素。

turns.en: The first ever essay I wrote when I was doing my international relations degree was we were allowed to choose our own topic. And I chose like a Nietzschean interpretation of international relations, which I thought at the time was just me being like an insufferable university student. But then I'm sure I was. I'm sure I was. But then I read End of History or the Nietzsche reference. And I was like, maybe I'm on to something.
turns.zh: 我在读国际关系学位时写的第一篇文章——当时我们可以自己选题——我选了一个 Nietzsche 式的国际关系解读，当时我觉得那只是我作为一个令人难以忍受的大学生在装腔作势。但我确实是。我确实是。但后来我读了 End of History 里面关于 Nietzsche 的引用，我就想，也许我发现了什么。

turns.en: Maybe maybe you're on to something. OK, one interpretation of many of the political events that have transpired, I suppose, is that people got bored. Right. And so there's obviously more than the German election. There is the election of Donald Trump and there is Brexit and actually like a million other things that we could cite within what we call liberalism. We grew up with or learned to celebrate differences among people and that this was important and pluralism and difference and diversity and all these things that were like internalized as positive. But I sometimes wonder, is there like a contradiction in the sense like we value pluralism and difference, but maybe some people really are different in the sense that like, no, like they really want a different order or they really want to live in a distinct culture and that maybe is less oriented towards the market, et cetera, really more energized by the idea of cultural homogeneity or something like that. From the sort of liberal perspective, how do you think about difference? Because things like migration, et cetera, seem to be one of the through lines for all of this sort of illiberal, the rise of illiberalism.
turns.zh: 也许也许你确实发现了什么。好，对已经发生的诸多政治事件的一种解读，我想，就是人们觉得无聊了。对吧。所以显然不只是德国选举。还有 Donald Trump 的当选，还有 Brexit，实际上还有无数其他我们可以列举的事情。在我们所说的自由主义框架内，我们从小被教导要庆祝人与人之间的差异，这很重要——多元主义（pluralism）、差异和多样性——所有这些都被内化为正面的东西。但我有时想知道，是否存在一种矛盾：我们重视多元和差异，但也许有些人真的是不同的——他们的意思是，不，他们真的想要一种不同的秩序，或者真的想生活在一种独特的文化中，那种文化也许不那么面向市场等等，更多是被文化同质性（cultural homogeneity）的概念所激励。从自由主义的角度，你怎么看待'差异'？因为像移民等问题似乎是所有这种非自由主义崛起的共同线索之一。

turns.en: No, that's exactly right. I think right from the beginning of liberalism, One of the charges has been it weakens community. It weakens the sense of togetherness, you know, shared values and so forth. And that's deliberate. Liberalism got its start in the 17th century after the European wars of religion, when Christians were killing each other over things like transubstantiation or childhood baptism. And the early liberals said, look, we actually need to accept the fact that we don't agree on the highest things. Let's just tolerate one another and live peacefully. And that's really the essence of liberalism. As you say, it accepts pluralism and difference. But I think that that's also what drives a lot of people crazy is that you have to tolerate people you really disagree with. And you don't get the strong sense that everybody is marching in the same direction. And I think, you know, that's the origin of nationalism. That's the origin of religious politics. the trouble is that people forget that this sort of politics is what gets you into trouble. 20th century was all about really strong national identities that wanted to assert themselves and dominate their neighbors. And you had two world wars as a result of it. Today, you see that in Vladimir Putin, right? That he's not content just to have a peaceful, prosperous Russia. He also has this idea that, you know, Russia is this great, you know, country that includes Ukraine and Belarus and all these other territories. And he, is not happy unless he's dominating all of that. And that is not compatible with a liberalism that says, you know, you got to live and let live.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。我认为从自由主义诞生之初，它面临的指控之一就是它削弱了共同体。它削弱了那种团结感——共享价值观等等。而这是刻意为之的。自由主义起源于17世纪欧洲宗教战争之后，当时基督徒因为变质说（transubstantiation）或婴儿洗礼这样的事情互相残杀。早期的自由主义者说，听着，我们其实需要接受一个事实：我们在最高层面的事情上并不一致。让我们互相宽容、和平共处吧。这才是自由主义的本质。正如你说的，它接受多元主义和差异。但我认为这也正是让很多人抓狂的地方——你必须容忍你真正不赞同的人。你得不到那种所有人都在朝同一个方向前进的强烈感觉。我认为，这就是民族主义的起源，也是宗教政治的起源。问题在于人们忘记了这种政治恰恰是让你陷入麻烦的东西。20世纪全都是关于非常强烈的民族认同想要 asserting 自己并支配邻国。结果就是两次世界大战。今天，你在 Vladimir Putin 身上看到了这一点，对吧？他不满足于拥有一个和平繁荣的 Russia。他还有这种想法：Russia 是一个伟大的国家，应该包括 Ukraine、Belarus 和所有这些其他领土。除非他支配着所有这些，否则他不会开心。这与一种主张'自己活也让别人活'的自由主义是不相容的。

turns.en: So setting aside multiculturalism for a second, which is a thorny problem for liberal democracies, I think you point to something in your book that to me is possibly an even thornier problem. It's this concept called megalithemia. Am I saying that right?
turns.zh: 那暂时先放下多元文化主义（multiculturalism）不谈——这对自由民主来说是个棘手问题——我觉得你在书中指出了一个对我来说可能更加棘手的问题。就是这个叫做 megalothymia 的概念。我读对了吗？

turns.en: Megalithemia, right.
turns.zh: Megalothymia，对。

turns.en: Megalithemia.
turns.zh: Megalothymia。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Which is like the desire to be recognized as superior. in some way. So people aren't just satisfied that they're all equal, they all have equal dignity, equal rights. People want to feel like they're special or superior in some way. And to me, Twitter, the fact that Twitter exists is.
turns.zh: 也就是某种想要被承认为优越的欲望。人们并不满足于大家都是平等的、都有平等的尊严和权利。人们想要觉得自己是特别的，或者在某种程度上是优越的。而对我来说，Twitter——Twitter 存在这件事本身——

turns.en: Like proof of this concept. That's exactly where my mind went.
turns.zh: 就是这个概念的证据。我的想法完全一样。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: You know, you have people like Elon Musk, the richest man in the world, who still wants a platform to be heard and feel superior to others.
turns.zh: 你看，像 Elon Musk 这样的人，世界上最富有的人，仍然想要一个平台来被听到、来感觉自己比别人优越。

turns.en: When I went and re-read The End of History several years ago, All I could think about is this explains why so many billionaires who have all the power in the world, what they really crave deep down at the base of that Maslow's Pyramid is to be listened to and respected. And it drives them crazy that they have everything, but they are still not as influential as a typical up-end columnist. And I think this is the source of tremendous psychological angst, even for the most powerful people.
turns.zh: 几年前我重新读 The End of History 时，我满脑子想的都是：这解释了为什么那么多拥有世间一切权力的亿万富翁，他们内心深处真正渴望的——在 Maslow 金字塔的底层——是被倾听和被尊重。他们拥有一切，但影响力还不如一个典型的专栏作家，这让他们抓狂。我认为这就是即便最有权势的人也承受巨大心理焦虑的根源。

turns.en: In the world.
turns.zh: 在这世上。

turns.en: All right, now imagine that on a society-wide scale. Everyone wants to feel superior and recognized in some way. How are liberal democracies supposed to deal with that?
turns.zh: 好吧，现在把这个想象成整个社会层面的问题。每个人都想以某种方式感到优越和被认可。自由民主政体应该如何应对这个问题？

turns.en: So just as a footnote, I mentioned Donald Trump in the original End of History and the Last Man book. At that point, I said the great thing about having a capitalist democracy is that there's a way of bleeding off some of that desire to dominate and be great because you can just get rich. And I gave Donald Trump as an example. Little did I know that just getting rich wasn't enough for him, that he also wanted the political glory. So I don't think you can get away from megalothumia, this desire to be recognized as greater because That's the source of any excellence. You know, if you want to be a great pianist or a great football forward or a great athlete or anything, you have to have this will to excel and to be better than other people. The trouble is that it oftentimes leads in bad directions where you simply want to be a tyrant. And I think you're right that, you know, if you're a billionaire, there's no material need that you have unsatisfied. What you don't have is the recognition of other people, of other billionaires that And I think that's really what's driving a lot of the competition in our economy. If it just stayed economic competition, that would be fine. But when it becomes politicized and turns into political ambition, I think that's where democracy gets in trouble. And I think that's really the challenge that we're facing. You're also correct that I think on a national level, people want this feeling of togetherness. They want a sense of national identity that is stronger than just tolerating everybody. And that is one of the reasons we still have conflicts in the world today.
turns.zh: 作为一个脚注，我在最初那本 The End of History and the Last Man 中就提到了 Donald Trump。当时我说，拥有资本主义民主的一个好处是，有一种方式可以释放掉部分支配欲和伟大欲——因为你可以去发财。我举了 Donald Trump 作为例子。我没想到光发财对他来说不够，他还想要政治荣耀。所以我不认为你能摆脱 megalothymia——这种被认可为更伟大的欲望——因为那是一切卓越的源泉。如果你想成为伟大的钢琴家、伟大的足球前锋、伟大的运动员或任何东西，你必须有这种追求卓越、要比别人更好的意志。问题是它常常导向不好的方向——你只是想当一个暴君。我认为你说得对：如果你是亿万富翁，没有什么是你物质上未得到满足的。你没有的是其他人的认可——其他亿万富翁的认可。我认为这才是真正驱动我们经济中大量竞争的东西。如果它只停留在经济竞争层面，那没问题。但当它被政治化、变成政治野心时，我认为那就是民主陷入麻烦的地方。我认为这确实是我们面临的挑战。你说的也对：在国家层面，人们想要那种团结感。他们想要一种比仅仅容忍所有人更强烈的民族认同感。这也是当今世界仍有冲突的原因之一。

turns.en: When you think about the events of the last 40 years or 20 years, maybe. Something that I'm very interested in, I'm curious whether you think about it much, is the changing media environment and the degree to which, say, for better or worse, you have a few monopoly media outlets, and that has this sort of effect of everyone having the same diet. And I'm curious, the role of digital media and social media and your active Instagram user in sort of regrouping people around, I guess might people say like tribal lines and this bit, the way technology changes how we interact and relate to each other.
turns.zh: 当你思考过去40年或20年的事件时——有一个我非常感兴趣的东西，我好奇你是否经常思考——就是媒体环境的变化。在某种程度上，不管好坏，你有几个垄断性的媒体 outlet，这产生了所有人'吃同样的精神食粮'的效果。我好奇的是数字媒体和社交媒体的角色——你是一个活跃的 Instagram 用户——以及它们在把人们重新按部落化（tribal）的路线分组方面所起的作用，技术如何改变了我们互动和彼此关联的方式。

turns.en: I think it's had a really profound effect. One of the most dangerous for democracies is the fact that we no longer agree about simple empirical facts because, you know, the old media really had certain journalistic standards. You couldn't just publish anything. Your editor would say, well, do you have a second source on that? And if you didn't, you know, it wouldn't get in the newspaper. Today, you know, we have the internet where anyone can say anything. And not only can they say anything, but that anything can be amplified. There's a, I think, very unhealthy dynamic in the online world where you get noticed. If you're an internet influencer, you say something sensible or Rational reasonable, you know people will listen to you, but.
turns.zh: 我认为它产生了非常深远的影响。对民主最危险的一点是，我们不再对简单的经验事实达成一致了。因为你知道，传统媒体确实有一定的新闻标准。你不能随便发任何东西。你的编辑会说：嗯，这个有第二个信源吗？如果没有，它就上不了报纸。今天呢，我们有了互联网，任何人都可以说任何话。而且不仅可以说任何话，那些话还能被放大。我认为网络世界中有一种非常不健康的'获取关注'的动态：如果你是网络 influencer，你说了一些明智的、理性的、合理的话，人们会听你的，但是——

turns.en: They won't my take bring back earnestness on the internet It's so out of fashion if you say something reasonable and earnest It's like immediately consigned to the realms of internet.
turns.zh: 他们不会听的。我的看法是：把真诚（earnestness）带回互联网吧。它太不时髦了——如果你说了什么合理又真诚的话，它立刻就被打入互联网的冷宫了。

turns.en: But there's an inevitable dynamic that happens where the moment you start saying something unreasonable, you know, you insult somebody or you say something that's just ridiculously untrue it sets off, you know, a big uptick in your followers. And then you say, okay, we got to top that by saying something even more extreme. And I think that that explains a lot of the extremism in our politics because people are living in an online world and they also don't agree on basic facts.
turns.zh: 但有一种不可避免的动态：一旦你开始说不合理的话——比如侮辱某人或者说一些荒谬的不实之言——你的粉丝量就会大幅上升。然后你想：好吧，我们得说更极端的话来超越那个。我认为这解释了我们政治中的很多极端主义，因为人们生活在网络世界里，而且他们连基本事实都不一致。

turns.en: Since we're on the topic of, I guess, new media and technology, can we talk a little bit about AI?
turns.zh: 既然我们在聊新媒体和技术的话题，我们能谈谈 AI 吗？

turns.en: Speaking of The Last Man.
turns.zh: 说到 The Last Man。

turns.en: Speaking of The Last Man. I knew there was an AI chapter in your new book, and I thought it was going to be more about, I guess, like the existential threat of AI and what it means for the whole bored last man concept. But you talk about it in a sort of state administrative sense. capacity way. Why did you decide to take that line as opposed to, I don't know, arguing how AI would fit into the socio-political economy more broadly?
turns.zh: 说到 The Last Man。我知道你的新书里有一章关于 AI，我以为它会更多地讨论 AI 的存在性威胁（existential threat），以及它对整个'无聊的末人'概念意味着什么。但你是从一种国家行政能力的角度来谈的。为什么你决定走那条路线，而不是——我不知道——论证 AI 如何更广泛地融入社会政治经济？

turns.en: Well, no, I think that what I said was that the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI. That is where human beings delegate to machines the power to make decisions. And I spent a lot of time thinking about human hierarchies. And I know that we often over-delegate authority in organizations and governments. But I think we're beginning to do that. I think this Hugging Face incident that OpenAI got into where they had developed an AI agent that broke out of its playpen and then started getting out into the internet and breaking into other computers, that's what agentic AI is all about. And that's what I think the whole loss of control fear is related to, is that you're going to create these agents that are powerful. And the thing about modern AI is that the people that create them don't really understand what's going on underneath the hood. Classic computer programming, line by line, it's very deterministic what the computer is going to do. With these new AIs, they don't really understand why it's behaving the way it is. And if you then delegate authority to a machine where you don't really know why it's thinking what it's thinking, I think that's what leads you down the road to some real doomer scenarios where they can kind of act as if they've got their own volitions and really no human being is going to be able to control them.
turns.zh: 嗯，不，我认为我说的是 AI 最危险的方面是 agentic AI（自主代理式 AI）。就是人类把决策权委托给机器。我花了大量时间思考人类等级制度。我知道我们在组织和政府中经常过度授权。但我认为我们正在开始对机器做这件事。我觉得 OpenAI 碰到的那个 Hugging Face 事件——他们开发了一个 AI agent，它突破了围栏，然后开始闯入互联网、侵入其他计算机——那就是 agentic AI 的核心问题。我认为整个'失控'的恐惧与此相关：你将要创造出这些强大的 agent。而现代 AI 的问题在于，创造它们的人其实并不真正理解底层发生了什么。经典计算机编程是逐行的，计算机要做什么是非常确定性的。但对于这些新 AI，他们其实不理解它为什么表现出那样的行为。如果你把权力委托给一台你并不真正知道它为什么那样思考的机器，我认为那就是通往真正的末日场景（doomer scenarios）的道路——它们可能表现得像有自己的意志，而没有任何人类能够控制它们。

turns.en: You're a famous tinker and you like building stuff and you do woodworking, et cetera. Do you tinker with AI? Do you play around with it the way you play around with like making bookshelves or working on a car engine or something like that?
turns.zh: 你是出了名的爱折腾，喜欢动手做东西，做木工之类的。你会折腾 AI 吗？你会像做书架或修汽车引擎那样去玩 AI 吗？

turns.en: Well, ever since the early 90s, I built my own computers and I've written my own software and I use cloud code a lot. It's just an amazing thing. I mean, I had written some fairly complicated programs, but I got stuck.
turns.zh: 嗯，从90年代初开始，我就自己组装电脑、自己写软件，而且我现在大量使用 Claude Code。它真的是太神奇了。我是说，我之前写了一些相当复杂的程序，但卡住了。

turns.en: What kind of stuff were you building?
turns.zh: 你在做什么样的东西？

turns.en: Well, I mean, mostly it was, I have, I maintain a few big databases on some servers that I keep at home and I wanted to migrate it to a different system and cloud code just did it. You know, you, you, you don't, I mean, it helps to be a programmer cause you can then correct things where it makes mistakes, but, uh, yeah, basically it's, it's just an amazing system.
turns.zh: 嗯，主要是这样：我在家里有几台服务器，上面维护着一些大型数据库，我想把它们迁移到另一个系统，Claude Code 直接就搞定了。你知道，你不需要——我是说，会编程是有帮助的，因为你可以纠正它犯错的地方，但是，嗯，是的，基本上它就是一个了不起的系统。

turns.en: There's a picture in the book of one of the tables that you made, and it looks really nice. It looks like a legitimate table.
turns.zh: 你书里有一张你做的桌子的照片，看起来真不错。看起来像一张正经的桌子。

turns.en: It's beautiful. It is legitimate. You can really sit at it. So when I was in the State Department, the Secretary of State has a suite on the eighth floor that's beautiful. It's furnished with these antique federal-style American classic furniture. And when I was delivering memos up there as a young official officer, I really admired that and I wished I could have that in my own home. So basically I taught myself how to build this kind of furniture.
turns.zh: 它很漂亮。它是正经的。你真的可以坐在旁边用。我在国务院（State Department）工作时，国务卿在八楼有一套很漂亮的办公室。里面摆着这些古董联邦风格（Federal-style）的美式经典家具。当我作为一个年轻官员送备忘录上去的时候，我真的很欣赏那些家具，希望我自己家里也能有。所以基本上我自学了怎么做这种家具。

turns.en: I love that. I upholstered a chair recently for similar reasons, but I have yet to get to the actual woodworking of the chair itself.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个故事了。我最近也因为类似的原因给一把椅子做了软包（upholstery），但我还没有开始做椅子本身的木工。

turns.en: We could just talk woodworking and upholstery for the rest of the time.
turns.zh: 我们接下来可以一直聊木工和软包了。

turns.en: Could you do a Chippendale chair, you think?
turns.zh: 你觉得你能做一把 Chippendale 风格的椅子吗？

turns.en: I don't like the Chippendale style that much. I like Federal because it's a little bit cleaner.
turns.zh: 我不太喜欢 Chippendale 风格。我更喜欢 Federal 风格，因为它更简洁一些。

turns.en: Cleaner and simpler.
turns.zh: 更简洁、更简单。

turns.en: Still decorated. It's got inlay and I think that's about my favorite, you know, style of furniture. When you get into things like empire, you know, then that becomes really a different level of skill because you have to carve all these, you know, dragons and faces and things into the woodwork. And that's something I never got into. All right.
turns.zh: 但仍有装饰。它有镶嵌工艺（inlay），我觉得那大概是我最喜欢的家具风格了。当你进入 Empire 风格之类的，那就真的是另一个层次的技艺了，因为你得在木头上雕刻各种龙、面孔之类的东西。那是我从来没涉足的领域。好吧。

turns.en: At the risk of turning this into an interior design episode. No.
turns.zh: 冒着把这期变成室内设计专题的风险。不要。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Serious question. Just going back to AI. But what does AI actually mean for the last man in concept itself? Do you see, because I feel like you could go in two directions, and we've done episodes on both these scenarios. You could have one where people just become even more nihilistic and filled with ennui, so to speak, or you could maybe have a sort of utopian world where AI is doing all the work for us and we get freed up to pursue some of our cultural pursuits.
turns.zh: 严肃问题。回到 AI。但 AI 对'末人'这个概念本身意味着什么？你觉得——因为我觉得可能有两个方向，我们做过关于这两种情景的节目——一种是人变得更加虚无主义（nihilistic）、充满倦怠（ennui）；另一种也许是一个乌托邦世界，AI 帮我们做了所有工作，我们被解放出来去追求文化活动。

turns.en: Yeah, actually, that was John Maynard Keynes' vision of the future, that productivity would increase so much that we'd have, you know, we'd only have to work 10, 20 hours a week and the rest we could pursue hobbies and so forth. I don't think that's going to make people happy in the end. I mean, same problem with universal basic income. And the reason for this has to do with this concept of thumos. So megalothumia comes from this Greek word thumos, which is spiritedness or pride, that in addition to material needs, human beings want to be recognized for their basic human dignity and And quite frankly, a lot of our dignity comes from the work we do. The fact that you are paid to do a job means that somebody in society thinks that what you do is valuable enough to give you money for it. And I think that that's why this vision of a society where everybody is just, you know, selling trinkets on Etsy, but not really, you know, doing the kind of work that we're used to doing. it's not going to make people happy because it doesn't give them a sense of pride and accomplishment. You know, that it's, you could spend your whole life playing video games. And I think part of the reason that you got this manosphere that is so, you know, restless is that's what they do. You know, they're online all the time. They have all these fantasies about being, you know, superheroes, but in real life, they kind of know that, you know, there's this basic emptiness there. And I think that that lack of, work that gives you dignity that ordinary people can feel is one of the things that may be destroyed by AI because it's so capable of substituting for that kind of human labor. And I think that's really one of the big dangers because either people will be perpetually lonely and unhappy or they will rebel against that and you'll have a lot of political turmoil.
turns.zh: 是的，其实那就是 John Maynard Keynes 对未来的愿景：生产力会增长到如此程度，我们每周只需要工作10到20个小时，剩下的时间可以追求爱好等等。我不认为这最终会让人快乐。我是说，全民基本收入（universal basic income）也有同样的问题。原因跟 thumos 这个概念有关。Megalothymia 来自希腊词 thumos，意思是血气（spiritedness）或自豪感。除了物质需求之外，人类希望自己的基本人格尊严被认可。而且坦率地说，我们的很多尊严来自我们做的工作。你做一份工作并获得报酬，这意味着社会中有人认为你做的事有足够价值来为此付钱给你。我认为这就是为什么那种'每个人都在 Etsy 上卖小玩意儿，但并不真正做我们习惯的那种工作'的社会愿景不会让人快乐——因为它不给人自豪感和成就感。你可以花一辈子打游戏。我认为 manosphere（男性圈）如此躁动不安的部分原因就是——那就是他们在做的事。他们一直在线，有各种关于成为超级英雄的幻想，但在现实生活中，他们大概知道那里有一种根本性的空虚。我认为，那种能给普通人尊严感的工作的缺失，是可能被 AI 摧毁的东西之一，因为 AI 太擅长替代那种人类劳动了。我认为这确实是最大的危险之一：要么人们永远孤独和不快乐，要么他们会反抗，然后你就会有大量的政治动荡。

turns.en: There's so many different things sort of working against quote, liberalism, etc. And there are people arguing for it, right? Like there's communities of people online who like try to like argue about these things and argue we should be building things and appreciate markets and appreciate prosperity. But it's all a little hollow. It doesn't seem like really fully scratch that itch. Like we can get there intellectually. OK, these are good things, but it doesn't supply that sort of like spiritedness, etc., Does anyone out there have conceptions of what a positive vision for liberalism or counter-illiberalism looks like other than, no, look, GDP goes up. Look, actually, things haven't been getting worse. Actually, despite what you see online, real wages generally have been rising. These arguments may or may not be true, but they certainly don't seem to satisfy many people. They don't excite people. It's not something that you really get behind enthusiastically. Do you see anyone or any path of like, oh, this is what a reinvigorated vision looks like?
turns.zh: 有很多不同的东西在对抗所谓的'自由主义'等等。也有人在为它辩护，对吧？网上有一些社区的人在试图讨论这些问题，主张我们应该建设东西、欣赏市场、欣赏繁荣。但这一切都有点空洞。它似乎并没有真正挠到那个痒处。我们在理智上可以到达那里——好的，这些是好东西——但它并不提供那种血气等等。有没有人有关于自由主义或反非自由主义的正面愿景是什么样的构想？除了'不，看，GDP 在涨'、'看，其实事情并没有变差'、'其实尽管你在网上看到的，实际工资总体一直在上升'——这些论点可能真也可能不真，但它们显然不能满足很多人。它们不能让人兴奋。不是你真正会热情拥护的东西。你有没有看到任何人或任何路径表明——哦，这就是一个重新焕发生机的愿景？

turns.en: Well, there are some possible futures where you actually do face real threats, where the society really does have to mobilize. I think we felt something like that in the 1930s with the Depression and then fighting World War II, and that was very inspiring to many people. It was also very devastating. And the question is, can you recreate that sense of national purpose without having a war or pandemic or revolution? I think you can. I think that there are a lot of projects out there in the world that could be the source of a greater sense of common purpose. One of the themes in the book is indeed the fact that we don't build anything anymore. I live in California. We were promised high-speed rail. They allocated money for it in the mid-1990s, and we have like 10 miles of track in the Central Valley where nobody lives. And I think that you could actually recreate some of that sense of purpose if you could get back to actually having projects that are big and visible. That's part of what the Chinese government has been doing. They are really good at building infrastructure. They build these incredible bridges over gorges in the middle of the interior of China, but it actually adds to the sense that The society is moving forward and it's accomplished something, plus which I'd like to be able to get from L.A. to San Francisco in three hours. It would be pretty convenient if you could do that.
turns.zh: 嗯，有一些可能的未来是你确实面临真正的威胁，社会确实需要动员起来。我想我们在1930年代大萧条和随后打二战时感受过类似的东西，那对很多人来说是非常鼓舞人心的。同时也是非常具有毁灭性的。问题是：你能不能在没有战争、大流行病或革命的情况下重建那种国家使命感？我认为可以。我认为世界上有很多项目可以成为更强烈的共同使命感的来源。书中的主题之一确实是我们不再建设任何东西了。我住在 California。他们承诺了高铁（high-speed rail）。1990年代中期就拨了款，而我们在 Central Valley——一个没人住的地方——只有大约10英里的铁轨。我认为如果你能重新拥有大型且可见的项目，你确实可以重建那种使命感。这也是中国政府一直在做的事情的一部分。他们非常擅长建设基础设施。他们在中国内地的峡谷上建造了令人难以置信的桥梁，这确实增加了社会在前进、在成就什么的感觉。而且，我希望能从 L.A. 到 San Francisco 只花三个小时。如果能做到那会很方便。

turns.en: As soon as you brought up America's lack of high-speed rail, I knew my next question was going to be about China. But talk to us a little bit more about China, because if we think that liberal democracy has won in some way, it's the inevitable outcome of human evolution. People can still point to China and say, well, that's not a liberal democracy. That is something else. And it seems to be reasonably successful at this moment in time, at least when judging by infrastructure projects like high-speed rail.
turns.zh: 你一提到美国缺少高铁，我就知道我的下一个问题一定是关于中国的。多跟我们聊聊 China 吧，因为如果我们认为自由民主在某种意义上已经赢了——它是人类演化的必然结果——人们仍然可以指着 China 说：嗯，那不是自由民主，那是另一种东西。而且它在此时此刻看起来相当成功，至少从基础设施项目比如高铁来判断是这样。

turns.en: Yeah. know, I've been saying this for several decades, that the only alternative society that is not a liberal democracy that looks like a plausible competitor is China, because they are able to stay at the frontier of technology, they've maintained social stability, and they certainly have great GDP growth numbers. So the question is, is that going to be a sustainable model going forward? And I don't think the answer is fully in. I mean, right now, the US versus China, we don't look so good. I think very few people around the world are saying, well, we want to be polarized and angry and at each other's throats all the time. And they look at China and they do see the modern cities and infrastructure that's come up virtually overnight. I think, however, it is a little bit premature to declare that they've won that contest because there are some big problems, both in the economic model and in the political model. As far as the economic model is concerned, I think Xi Jinping actually made a big mistake after he came to power because instead of investing in the interior of China in social services and pensions and so forth, he decided to double down on this export-led growth This time driven by high tech and it's destroying the manufacturing base of every other society in the world. You know, what happened to the United States in the early two thousands, the Europeans may lose their auto industry, you know, as a result of Chinese EVs and it's producing a big, big backlash and the rest of the economy actually is not doing well. They have this big property bust and they're still not out of it. Uh, the amount of unemployment for Chinese young people is really pretty dramatic. And it's just going to get worse as they introduce AI into their economy. So we'll have to see. The political model has done better than I would have expected. The idea is as you get richer, better educated, you're not content simply to be a passive subject. You actually want to participate. You want to be able to express your opinion. And you can't do that in China. And I think that there still may come a point where that unhappiness is going to come out expressed politically. It's a very effective dictatorship that right now can squash any signs of discontent. But, you know, that may not be the case forever.
turns.zh: 是的。你知道，我几十年来一直在说，唯一一个不是自由民主但看起来像是一个可信竞争者的替代社会就是 China，因为他们能够保持在技术前沿，维持了社会稳定，GDP 增长数字也确实亮眼。所以问题是，这种模式在未来是否可持续？我认为答案还没有完全揭晓。我是说，现在 US 对比 China，我们看起来不太好。我想世界上很少有人会说'嗯，我们想要极化、愤怒、一直互相掐架'。他们看着 China，确实看到了几乎一夜之间崛起的现代化城市和基础设施。然而我认为，宣称他们赢得了这场竞赛还为时过早，因为经济模式和政治模式都存在一些大问题。就经济模式而言，我认为 Xi Jinping 上台后实际上犯了一个大错误：他没有投资于中国内地的社会服务和养老金等等，而是决定加倍押注出口导向型增长——这一次由高科技驱动——这正在摧毁世界上其他所有社会的制造业基础。你知道，US 在2000年代初发生的事情，Europeans 可能因为中国 EV 而失去他们的汽车工业，这正在引发巨大的反弹。而且其余经济实际上表现不佳。他们有巨大的房地产崩盘，而且还没有走出来。中国年轻人的失业率确实相当惊人。而且随着他们在经济中引入 AI，情况只会变得更糟。所以我们拭目以待。政治模式的表现比我预期的要好。这个理念是：当你变得更富有、受教育程度更高时，你不会满足于只做一个被动的臣民。你实际上想要参与，想要能够表达自己的意见。而在中国你做不到这一点。我认为可能仍然会有某个时刻，那种不满会以政治的方式表达出来。这是一个非常有效的独裁政权，目前可以压制任何不满的迹象。但你知道，这种情况未必能永远持续。

turns.en: We have no idea what the future holds. But here in 2026, there are a number of, China is the main example, but there are a number of places that are not, quote, democracies that seem to be stable. And some of the Gulf countries have obviously done extraordinarily well over the past couple of decades. Have you revisited any of your premises about this idea that an educated elite eventually really wants a say, that they actually want to be stakeholders in politics? Or is there a degree of like if you have competent management or if you're perceived to have competent management, maybe that just doesn't manifest as a problem?
turns.zh: 我们不知道未来会怎样。但在2026年的当下，有很多——China 是主要的例子——但有很多不是所谓的'民主'的地方看起来很稳定。一些海湾国家在过去几十年显然表现得非常好。你有没有重新审视过你的前提——关于受过教育的精英最终真的想要发言权、真的想成为政治的利益相关者这个观点？或者说，如果你有——或者被认为有——称职的管理，也许那种问题就不会显现出来？

turns.en: I think that I'm perfectly willing to accept the fact that there are different models. Certainly the American one compared even to other rich democracies has a lot of problems in the way we organize our institutions that have led to some of the instability that we see. I think that the question about real authoritarian alternatives, you know, Singapore is the one that's brought up all the time. I'm perfectly happy to admit that the Singaporeans govern themselves pretty well. But the question is first, can you actually export that model to other countries? You know, if you had a regular source of Lee Kuan Yew that you could call on to run your authoritarian country, that would be great. But most authoritarian countries end up with a Lukashenko or Putin or a really bad leader. And that's the problem with that kind of concentration of power. The longer term question is the one that you pointed to is, are people simply willing to be passive consumers who are satisfied with just the stability offered by a Singaporean type government? And that's where I think you do get into this last man question, because Nietzsche would say, no, human beings want to aim higher than that. You know, they want to struggle for things and eventually they're not going to be happy with, you know, the kind of peace and prosperity that an authoritarian government can offer. At least in our liberal society, we can have an active civil society. So you can believe what you want. You can get together with other people. You can pursue all sorts of ambitions as long as they're not ones that want to dominate, you know, the rest of the society. And in a place like China, that's much more limited.
turns.zh: 我完全愿意接受存在不同模式这个事实。当然，美国的模式——即使与其他富裕民主国家相比——在我们组织制度的方式上有很多问题，导致了我们所看到的一些不稳定。关于真正的威权替代方案——Singapore 是经常被提起的那个。我完全乐意承认新加坡人把自己治理得相当好。但问题是：第一，你能把那种模式输出到其他国家吗？如果你有一个稳定的 Lee Kuan Yew 供应源可以请来管理你的威权国家，那太好了。但大多数威权国家最终得到的是 Lukashenko 或 Putin 或一个非常糟糕的领导人。那就是这种权力集中的问题。更长远的问题就是你指出的那个：人们是否愿意仅仅做被动的消费者，满足于 Singapore 式政府提供的稳定？这就是我认为你确实会触及'末人'问题的地方，因为 Nietzsche 会说：不，人类想要追求更高的目标。他们想要为某些东西奋斗，最终他们不会满足于威权政府能提供的和平与繁荣。至少在我们的自由社会里，我们可以有一个活跃的公民社会（civil society）。你可以信仰任何你想信仰的。你可以和其他人聚在一起。你可以追求各种抱负，只要它们不是想要支配社会其他部分的。而在像 China 这样的地方，这就受限得多了。

turns.en: So on China specifically, there's an anecdote that you describe in your book where you get to meet with the former vice president, Wang Qishan. And That's super interesting because it seems almost like you were summoned over there to talk to him and then he ended up just talking at you for about an hour. But what's your theory of what you were doing there? Was China trying to understand more about liberal politics or were they just trying to, I don't know, was it some sort of like internal CCP political game?
turns.zh: 具体说到 China，你在书中描述了一个轶事：你得以会见前副主席 Wang Qishan。这超级有意思，因为看起来几乎像是你被召去跟他谈话，然后他对着你讲了大约一个小时。但你的理论是什么——你去那里做什么？是 China 试图更多地了解自由主义政治，还是他们只是在——我不知道——那是某种 CCP 内部的政治博弈？

turns.en: Well, I don't know the answer to that. He definitely wanted to talk to me. He had read my book and So he was credited as being a genuine intellectual. Apparently, Xi Jinping was not all that happy with him because he was entertaining some rather heterodox ideas. He wanted, however, to talk to me. He was leading at that point this big anti-corruption campaign that Xi had unleashed, where they actually executed some very senior ministers and tens, if not hundreds of thousands of Communist Party officials were sacked. put in jail as a result of this. So he was the second most feared man and most powerful man in China. But I think he wanted to indicate that he was still open to the fact that a more liberal China might be possible in the future, but he still had to demonstrate his loyalty. It's a little bit of a contrast because the other dictator that I had encountered at that point was Muammar Gaddafi, who also invited me to Libya to talk to him. And I mean, it kind of explains why Libya is a mess and China is one of the great powers in the world because, you know, Gaddafi's head was totally uneducated. He really is somebody I felt in the end should have gone to college and actually gotten a decent education.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不知道答案。他确实想跟我谈。他读过我的书，所以他被认为是一个真正的知识分子。显然 Xi Jinping 对他不太满意，因为他在思考一些相当异端的想法。然而他想跟我谈谈。当时他正在领导 Xi 发起的大规模反腐运动——他们实际上处决了一些非常高级的部长，数万甚至数十万共产党官员被免职、入狱。所以他是中国最令人畏惧、最有权势的第二号人物。但我认为他想表明，他仍然对一种更自由化的 China 在未来成为可能持开放态度，但他仍然必须展示自己的忠诚。这形成了一个对比，因为我在那段时间遇到的另一个独裁者是 Muammar Gaddafi，他也邀请我去 Libya 跟他谈。我的意思是，这有点解释了为什么 Libya 一团糟而 China 是世界大国之一——因为 Gaddafi 的脑子完全没有受过教育。我真的觉得他最终应该去上大学，接受一些正规教育。

turns.en: His son famously went to LSE.
turns.zh: 他儿子 famously 去了 LSE。

turns.en: Well, his son was given a degree by LSE, whether he really went to LSE. And in fact, the, uh, the chancellor and his thesis advisor had to be sacked. Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，他儿子被 LSE 授予了学位，至于是他是否真的去了 LSE……事实上，校长和他的论文导师都被免职了。是的。

turns.en: Howard Davies. I remember this. I went to LSE.
turns.zh: Howard Davies。我记得这事。我就是 LSE 毕业的。

turns.en: Yeah. But that dictator was just, his head was full of conspiracy theories. And, you know, he believed that he had come up with the big alternative to communism and capitalism as a way forward, which was of course nonsense. Um, But, you know, Wang Qishan was a serious intellectual. He actually introduced Alexis de Tocqueville to China. So in Tocqueville's Old Regime and the Revolution, he explains that the French Revolution occurred not because of deprivation, but because France had started to reform itself in the generation before the revolution. Things were actually getting better, both economically and politically. But expectations were rising faster than the regime's ability to accommodate these new expectations. And that's why you had the revolution. And, you know, Wang Qishan's lesson was China shouldn't start down this road to liberalization the way Gorbachev had because that's just going to get, it's going to spiral out of control and the regime will fall. And that's what they did. And we have Alexis de Tocqueville to thank for the fact that they're still in power. Amazing.
turns.zh: 是的。但那个独裁者——他脑子里全是阴谋论。而且他相信自己想出了一个替代共产主义和资本主义的伟大前进道路，那当然是胡说八道。嗯，但是 Wang Qishan 是一个严肃的知识分子。他实际上把 Alexis de Tocqueville 引入了中国。在 Tocqueville 的 Old Regime and the Revolution（《旧制度与大革命》）中，他解释了法国大革命的发生不是因为匮乏，而是因为 France 在革命前一代开始了自我改革。事情实际上在经济和政治上都在变好。但期望的增长速度快于政权容纳这些新期望的能力。这就是为什么爆发了革命。Wang Qishan 的教训是：China 不应该像 Gorbachev 那样走上自由化的道路，因为那将会失控、螺旋式发展，政权会倒台。这就是他们做的。我们得感谢 Alexis de Tocqueville，他们才仍然在掌权。

turns.en: I want to talk about the neocons for a second. You've talked about how the sort of the aftermath of the war in Iraq and the aftermath led to a break between you and people who you may have seen as friends or ideological allies, etc. And yet, it seems to me that if we go and look at the sort of like cohort of people that we associate with like the neocon era in the early 2000s, particularly Iraq, Many of them today are some of the biggest defenders of, I guess, normal liberalism. You know, you think of like Dick Cheney, who, you know, like I don't think he supported Trump or Bill Kristol, who basically became a Democrat, et cetera. What do you make of this cohort that you could say 20, roughly 25 years ago was like there was a schism. They had like complete war. Terrible judgment, etc. And yet today, when you look at them, they are probably fairly aligned with you in terms of the sort of institutionalism and support for sort of the stability and the institutions that allowed America to thrive for a long time.
turns.zh: 我想聊一下新保守主义者（neocons）。你谈到过 Iraq 战争的后果如何导致了你和你可能视为朋友或意识形态盟友的人之间的决裂。然而在我看来，如果我们去看2000年代初我们所关联的新保守主义时代——特别是 Iraq——的那批人，他们中的许多人今天是正常自由主义最坚定的捍卫者。比如 Dick Cheney——我不认为他支持 Trump——或者 Bill Kristol，他基本上变成了一个民主党人，等等。你怎么看这批人？大约20到25年前有一场分裂，他们做了完全错误的判断等等。然而今天，当你看他们时，他们在制度主义（institutionalism）和支持让 America 长期繁荣的稳定与制度方面，可能和你相当一致。

turns.en: Well, to go a little bit into the intellect. history of that movement, a lot of people that were neocons back in the early 2000s had been second or third generation students of a German Jewish philosopher named Leo Strauss, who encouraged his students to think seriously about philosophy and about the philosophic ideas that You know, we're at the base of Western civilization. But the Straussians actually split into two different camps, East Coast and West Coast. The West Coast ones were followers of a student of Strauss named Harry Jaffa, who in the end, I think, could only be described as American nationalists because Jaffa regarded the American regime as the apotheosis of Aristotelian virtue. And those people went in the opposite direction. They became big Trump supporters. So Michael Anton, you know, the author of the famous Flight 93 article that served, you know, in both Trump administrations was, again, a product of that intellectual tradition. Bill Kristol and, as you mentioned, you know, Dick Cheney and especially his daughter Liz were very different and I think were more authentic believers in a constitutional Tradition that said the government power ought to be limited and that's what is really surprising to me about a lot of the conservatives that ended up supporting Trump because you know, they had built their ideological foundations around the idea of a rule of law and limitations Constitutional limits on government power. That's what it meant to be a conservative and yet, you know once their guy gets into power they want to take all those limits off and do everything through executive orders and flout the law if that's necessary to achieve their objectives. So I, you know, in the end, it's been a big puzzle to me why some people react to the same events with the same kind of educational background, but end up going in different ways. The only way I can explain it is in a way socially that you are not an objective scientist looking at facts. You are actually embedded in a social circle. And you're going to believe the things that people in your social circle believe.
turns.zh: 嗯，稍微深入一点那个运动的思想史：2000年代初很多新保守主义者是一位德国犹太哲学家 Leo Strauss 的第二或第三代学生，Strauss 鼓励他的学生认真思考哲学，思考那些处于西方文明基础的哲学理念。但 Straussians 实际上分裂成了两个阵营：东海岸和西海岸。西海岸的是 Strauss 的学生 Harry Jaffa 的追随者，我认为他们最终只能被描述为美国民族主义者（American nationalists），因为 Jaffa 把美国政体视为 Aristotelian 美德的极致体现。那些人走向了相反的方向——他们成了 Trump 的大力支持者。比如 Michael Anton——那篇著名的 Flight 93 文章的作者，在两届 Trump 政府中都任过职——同样是那个智识传统的产物。Bill Kristol，以及你提到的 Dick Cheney，特别是他的女儿 Liz，则非常不同。我认为他们是宪政传统（constitutional tradition）更真诚的信仰者——那种认为政府权力应该受到限制的传统。这才是真正让我惊讶的地方：很多最终支持 Trump 的保守派——他们的意识形态基础是围绕法治和对政府权力的宪法限制建立起来的。那就是做一个保守派的含义。然而一旦他们的人上台，他们就想解除所有限制，通过行政命令（executive orders）来做一切事情，如果有必要就蔑视法律来实现他们的目标。所以最终这对我来说是个大谜团：为什么有些人面对同样的事件、有着同样的教育背景，却走向了不同的方向。我唯一能解释的方式是从社会角度：你并不是一个客观审视事实的科学家。你实际上嵌入在一个社交圈子中。你会相信你的社交圈里的人所相信的东西。

turns.en: Just going back to, I guess, the overarching question of liberal democracy, you sort of end the book. It's not on a down note, but it's certainly on an uncertain note. You know, it's basically I'm not sure how to maintain liberal democracy or promote it. given that the message of liberal democracy doesn't seem to be resonating with a lot of people at the moment. So I'm just going to ask you directly, how should we, I guess, fix the PR of liberal democracy, or how would one go about actually doing that?
turns.zh: 回到自由民主这个总体问题——你在书的结尾，虽然不是以悲观收场，但确实是以一种不确定的基调收场。基本上就是：鉴于自由民主的信息目前似乎没有引起很多人的共鸣，我不确定如何维护或推广自由民主。所以我直接问你：我们应该如何修复自由民主的'公关形象'，或者说实际上该怎么做？

turns.en: Well, I think there's a twofold answer. I think we need to remind people about the dangers of the absence of liberal democracy. And you can see it right in the present world. Putin invades, does a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and gets into a bloody, bloody war that's now in its fifth year. That's what happens if you have a dictatorship instead of a liberal democracy. And then in a way, Ukraine, I think, is incredibly admirable because they want to defend their freedom and they're willing to die for it. And so there are inspiring causes. I think that the other part of the answer is that liberals need to actually have a positive program I don't think that you're going to beat back populism just by complaining about it, you know, bad as many of its programs and policies may be. I think that you have to offer people some positive vision for how their future is going to look different. And this gets back into this narrative about building things, you know, that liberal societies, one of the big problems that I talk about at the end is they accumulate too many rules. Liberalism is about a rule of law But you can actually have too much rule of law. So here in New York City, you know, rebuilding Wallman Link was almost impossible until Donald Trump took it over because, you know, there are just too damn many procedural requirements that you have to go through. And I think if government could actually be more effective and could actually carry through on its promises, you know, in a reasonable amount of time, people would start thinking, yeah, actually, this is working for me.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为答案有两个方面。第一，我们需要提醒人们没有自由民主的危险。你在当下的世界就能看到：Putin 全面入侵 Ukraine，陷入一场血腥的战争，现在已经进入第五年。那就是拥有独裁政权而非自由民主的后果。而且某种意义上，我认为 Ukraine 令人钦佩，因为他们想要捍卫自己的自由，并愿意为之而死。所以确实有鼓舞人心的事业。答案的另一部分是：自由主义者需要真正有一个正面的纲领。我不认为你仅仅通过抱怨就能击退民粹主义——尽管它的很多纲领和政策可能确实很糟糕。我认为你必须给人们提供一个正面的愿景，让他们看到未来会有什么不同。这又回到了关于建设东西的叙事。你知道，自由社会——我在书末讨论的一个大问题是它们积累了太多规则。自由主义讲的是法治（rule of law），但你实际上可能有太多法治。在 New York City，重建 Wollman Rink 几乎是不可能的，直到 Donald Trump 接管了它——因为你需要经过的程序要求实在太多了。我认为如果政府能真正更有效率，能在合理时间内兑现承诺，人们就会开始想：嗯，实际上这对我有用。

turns.en: It's tough to build things in the U.S. One area that it hasn't been difficult to build things in the U.S. is basically software and technology and all that. And you're, you know, at Stanford, you're kind of at ground zero for it. Granted, you're not, you know, in the computer science department, but I would just love to hear your perspective on how, you know, the culture of a university or the culture of students has changed maybe over the last couple of decades. with this sort of explosion of money and tech, et cetera, and how that, you know, how your students think about that and how that shapes the directions that they want to go in and whether it sort of bled over into some of the humanities or social sciences in some way.
turns.zh: 在美国建设东西很难。在美国建设东西不难的一个领域基本上是软件和技术。你在 Stanford，算是处于这场变革的核心地带。虽然你不在计算机科学系，但我很想听听你的看法：过去二十年来，随着科技和财富的爆发式增长，大学的文化或学生的文化是如何变化的？你的学生怎么看待这一点？它如何塑造了他们想要走的方向？它是否以某种方式渗透到了人文或社会科学领域？

turns.en: First of all, Stanford is different from Harvard and Yale because Harvard and Yale feed people into Wall Street, basically. You know, the smart, ambitious people all want to become billionaires through that route. At Stanford, they're more entrepreneurial. They want to do a startup that's then going to make them a billionaire. I think that in both places, it means that the humanities and social sciences are weak. You know, it's not the most favored route.
turns.zh: 首先，Stanford 跟 Harvard 和 Yale 不同，因为 Harvard 和 Yale 基本上是往 Wall Street 输送人才。聪明、有野心的人都想通过那条路成为亿万富翁。在 Stanford，他们更有创业精神。他们想做一个 startup 然后成为亿万富翁。我认为在两个地方，这意味着人文和社会科学都是弱势的。这不是最受青睐的路径。

turns.en: Do you feel it in some way with either the students that are coming through those departments or the interests of those students? Like, has it changed the texture of, like, professor-student relationship in some way in those departments?
turns.zh: 你是否有某种感受——无论是从那些院系的学生还是从学生的兴趣来看？它是否改变了那些院系中师生关系的质地？

turns.en: For me, I mean, I don't teach undergraduates anymore, so I'm a little bit.
turns.zh: 对我来说——我不再教本科生了，所以我有点——

turns.en: Removed from that.
turns.zh: 脱离那个了。

turns.en: But it's certainly the case that student politics has changed very dramatically, especially on the left, especially after October 7th and the Hamas attack. There's been a big radicalization of students, and they're mobilized around that issue and others that we're seeing in our national politics. So that's Certainly different. We went through this long period in the 90s and early 2000s of really student apathy. Everybody was too focused on getting a high paying job and they didn't really pay attention to politics. Now they're definitely more mobilized, but in some ways it's not a healthy mobilization because they're pursuing goals that I think are either unachievable or misguided, but they're definitely much more politically aware. I've got a number of students, you know, over the past decade that have actually gone into electoral politics. And I think that's great. I think that's what they ought to be doing.
turns.zh: 但学生政治确实发生了非常剧烈的变化，特别是左翼，特别是在10月7日 Hamas 袭击之后。学生出现了大幅激进化（radicalization），他们围绕那个议题和我们在国家政治中看到的其它议题被动员起来了。这当然不同了。我们在90年代和2000年代初经历了很长一段学生冷漠期。每个人都太专注于找一份高薪工作，不太关注政治。现在他们肯定更加被动员起来了，但在某些方面这不是一种健康的动员，因为他们在追求的目标我认为是不可实现的或方向错误的。但他们确实在政治上更加觉醒了。过去十年我有一些学生真正进入了选举政治。我认为这很好。我认为这才是他们应该做的事。

turns.en: Any advice for would-be international relations graduates?
turns.zh: 给有志于国际关系专业的毕业生有什么建议吗？

turns.en: Well, I think that you need to think broadly because right now international relations is extremely complicated as a disciplinary field because economics and sociology are absolutely at the core. You know, you want to know why you have global populism. Well, the sociology of most countries has changed. Left-wing parties are no longer based in working class populations. They've become basically parties of educated professionals who have very different political instincts than the working class. And part of the reason you've got this polarized politics both here and in Europe is because of that change. And that's not something, you know, in classical realist international theory, you don't look inside countries. You know, you just regard them as billiard balls. But if you don't see the domestic and the technological changes, and then by the way, the geopolitics of AI is really going to hit us, I think, like a freight train, because that's going to be one of the determining factors, just like nuclear weapons in a previous generation, about how power is going to be distributed in the coming world.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为你需要广泛地思考，因为现在国际关系作为一个学科领域极其复杂——经济学和社会学绝对处于核心位置。你想了解为什么有全球民粹主义？嗯，大多数国家的社会结构已经变了。左翼政党不再以工人阶级为基础。它们基本上变成了受过教育的专业人士的政党，这些人的政治直觉与工人阶级非常不同。你在这里和 Europe 都有极化政治的部分原因就是因为这种变化。这不是——在经典现实主义（classical realist）国际理论中你不会看国家内部。你只是把它们当作台球一样看待。但如果你看不到国内的变化和技术变化——而且顺便说一句，AI 的地缘政治（geopolitics of AI）真的会像一列货运火车一样撞击我们——因为那将是决定性因素之一，就像上一代的核武器一样，决定着权力在未来世界如何分配。

turns.en: That phenomenon of like, okay, the energy on the left coming from people who are not what people might have in a previously are called like the working class that many people are actually like fairly well to do and they're well educated. Is there, I mean, this is actually not even that new. I mean, right. Like historically, a lot of left movements have always had a certain many come from nobility or education or son of a wealthy business person, et cetera. Is this just people are different and that draws them to that? Or is there some sort of stronger theory or structural force that that has sort of like reinvigorated the sort of educated, successful left?
turns.zh: 那种现象——好的，左翼的能量来自那些不再是人们以前所称的工人阶级的人——很多人实际上相当富裕、受过良好教育。我是说，这其实并不是什么新鲜事。历史上很多左翼运动一直都有相当多的人来自贵族、受过教育的人、或者富商的子女等等。这只是因为人不同了、那种背景吸引了他们？还是有某种更强的理论或结构性力量重新激活了这个受过教育的、成功的左翼？

turns.en: Well, if I may, I think this is why this concept of the last man is important. You know, at Stanford, we had students that were living out in tents in an encampment after October 7th for six months. And you can't imagine a more privileged group of people than a Stanford undergrad, right? But, you know, I think what was missing in their lives was this sense that they were struggling and sacrificing for a higher cause of social justice. And that was the part that was missing in their lives. They'd struggled to get into Stanford, but it was just for themselves. And I think they wanted a more idealistic thing to aspire to. And I think that that's really what drives a lot of people into that kind of politics, is that they want to be able to risk their lives for something noble. And our liberal society doesn't give them a lot of opportunities for that kind of risk and daring.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果我可以说的话，我认为这就是为什么'末人'这个概念很重要。在 Stanford，10月7日之后有学生在露营地（encampment）里搭帐篷住了六个月。你想不出比 Stanford 本科生更特权的一群人了，对吧？但我认为他们生活中缺失的是那种他们在为社会正义这个更高事业奋斗和牺牲的感觉。那就是他们生活中缺失的部分。他们为了进入 Stanford 而奋斗过，但那只是为了自己。我认为他们想要一个更理想主义的东西去追求。我认为这才是真正驱动很多人进入那种政治的原因——他们想要能够为某些崇高的东西冒生命危险。而我们的自由社会并没有给他们太多这种冒险和大胆的机会。

turns.en: All right, Francis, this has been such a great conversation. Thank you so much for coming.
turns.zh: 好了，Francis，这是一次非常棒的对话。非常感谢你的到来。

turns.en: On All Thoughts.
turns.zh: 来到 All Thoughts。

turns.en: Thanks very much for having me.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你们的邀请。

turns.en: So, Joe, that was a lot of fun getting to interview a sort of legend, a legend in political economy. One thing that stood out to me, I find the idea of the last man and megalithemia or just themia in general very compelling because you look around you and you see that something does seem to be missing for a lot of people. And to me, it sort of boils down to a relativism versus absolutism kind of thing, which is like neo... neoliberalism or liberalism in general is predicated on this idea of absolute gain. So as long as everyone is kind of advancing, not necessarily at equal rates, as long as everyone is advancing in absolute terms, people should be happy. But my personal experience of life and the world and history is that actually people are very much relativist in nature. And it doesn't matter if everyone's advancing, if they're doing so at extremely different speeds or in very different ways. people aren't going to be happy. And I kind of, did you see that viral media thing? It was abundance, modern abundance.
turns.zh: Joe，能采访这样一位传奇人物——政治经济学界的传奇——真的太有趣了。让我印象深刻的一点是：我觉得'末人'和 megalothymia——或者说 thymos 整体——这个概念非常有说服力，因为你环顾四周就会看到很多人确实缺少了什么东西。对我来说，这归结为相对主义（relativism）与绝对主义（absolutism）的问题。就是说，新自由主义（neoliberalism）或一般意义上的自由主义是建立在绝对收益（absolute gain）这个理念之上的：只要每个人都在进步——不一定以相同的速率——只要每个人在绝对意义上都在前进，人们就应该快乐。但我个人对生活、世界和历史的体验是：人们实际上在本质上是非常相对主义的。即使每个人都在进步，如果他们以极其不同的速度或方式在进步，人们也不会快乐。你有没有看到那个病毒式传播的媒体内容？是关于 abundance 的——现代 abundance。

turns.en: Oh, I did see that.
turns.zh: 哦，我看到了。

turns.en: Where it was like, oh, everyone has a washing machine now.
turns.zh: 就是说，哦，现在每个人都有洗衣机了。

turns.en: Everyone has a toaster now, yeah. And they dreamed of this in the 1850s, that you could have crisp bread right on demand.
turns.zh: 每个人都有烤面包机了，是的。在1850年代人们就梦想这个——你可以随时有脆面包吃。

turns.en: It's all very true, but clearly it's not enough for people in 2026 that you can have a toaster and a washing machine and a TV and things like that.
turns.zh: 这都是事实，但显然对于2026年的人们来说，有一个烤面包机、一台洗衣机、一台电视之类的东西是不够的。

turns.en: You know, it's interesting. I forget who pointed it out, but someone pointed out like, that viral thing.
turns.zh: 你知道，很有意思。我忘了是谁指出的，但有人指出了那个病毒式传播的东西——

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: It didn't include like Instagram and phones because this is like one of the big things. It's not like, oh, and it's so great that we can now spend six hours scrolling reels all day, even though that is like one of the hallmark aspects of modernity.
turns.zh: 它没有包括 Instagram 和手机，因为这是最大的成就之一。不是说'哦，太好了，我们现在可以每天花六个小时刷 Reels'——尽管那确实是现代性的标志性特征之一。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Because people know it's not good and they know it's not satisfying and it's not something that ever like a hundred years ago.
turns.zh: 因为人们知道那不好，知道那不令人满足，那不是一百年前人们——

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Maybe you dream.
turns.zh: 也许会梦想——

turns.en: Of having a dishwasher.
turns.zh: 有一台洗碗机。

turns.en: You're doing fine, but you're looking at a picture of, I don't know, someone on a yacht and you're not doing as well as that.
turns.zh: 你过得不错，但你在看一张——我不知道——某人在游艇上的照片，然后觉得自己不如人家。

turns.en: Yeah, that that is it's meaningless. It's comparison is the thief of joy. All kinds of issues with that. But I totally this is why I always think about like the angry Twitter billionaires. Yeah, because it's like these people who have literally everything. And yet they're like driven crazy because they see a headline in the New York Times that they didn't like or something that they didn't agree with. And it drives them nuts. And I think that's just like, you know, there but for the grace of God, it's like, oh, like you have all this and yet you still can't find a way to achieve satisfaction because no one like really, you know, you're not like intellectually respected, et cetera. And you just see how that drives people crazy. And it is interesting too, like with the sort of utopian visions of AI, like, And the sort of paradox of all work is we want to work to achieve something, but we don't really, you don't want to finish. You don't want to like finish the goal. You don't want to actually end it because then you feel sort of, then what.
turns.zh: 是的，那毫无意义。比较是快乐的小偷。各种问题。但我完全理解——这就是为什么我总是想到那些愤怒的 Twitter 亿万富翁。是的，因为这些人拥有了一切，然而他们看到一条 New York Times 的标题不喜欢或者不同意什么就快被逼疯了。我觉得那就是——你知道——若非上帝恩典，就像：哦，你拥有这一切，但你仍然找不到获得满足的方法，因为没有人真正——你智力上没有受到尊重之类的。你就看到那如何把人逼疯。同样有趣的是关于 AI 的乌托邦愿景——以及所有工作的悖论：我们想要工作来实现某些东西，但我们其实不想完成。你不想达成目标。你不想真正结束它，因为那样你就会觉得——然后呢。

turns.en: Do you do? Well, I do kind of wonder, maybe AI can solve the last man problem in the sense that maybe if we have to feel superior and recognized- as humans. Maybe if we have offsetting AI agents and robots, we can feel superior to them.
turns.zh: 你——嗯，我确实有点好奇：也许 AI 能解决'末人'问题——从某种意义上说，如果我们作为人类需要感到优越和被认可，也许如果我们有对应的 AI agent 和机器人，我们可以对它们感到优越。

turns.en: It's hard to feel superior to them. That's part of the problem is like we're not going to feel that for very long. But yes, we could certainly try Chad GPT, solve the crisis of The Last Man, make no mistakes and see what it comes up with.
turns.zh: 很难对它们感到优越。这就是问题的一部分——我们不会有那种感觉很久。但是的，我们当然可以试试：ChatGPT，解决 The Last Man 的危机，不要犯错，看看它给出什么答案。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: Shall we leave it there?
turns.zh: 我们到此为止吧？

turns.en: Let's leave it there.
turns.zh: 就到这里吧。
